Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:6: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said in the name of Rabbi Shmuel: see the humility that is in the Holy One, blessed be He — what is written? (Ezekiel 44:2), "and the LORD said to me, this gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened" etc. A king of flesh and blood, his honor is to enter through a great gate — perhaps through a small gate? But the Holy One, blessed be He, enters in His glory through a small gate — hence, "and Your humility has made me great."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:7: Ben Azzai said: a king of flesh and blood, when he mentions his name, mentions his title first. But the Holy One, blessed be He, mentions His deeds first and afterward mentions His name, as it is said (Genesis 1:1), "in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:8: Another interpretation: "and You have given me the shield of Your salvation" — "fear not, Abram, I am a shield to you" (Genesis 15:1). "And Your right hand has supported me" — in the fiery furnace, among the kings, and in famine, as it is written, "the utterance of the LORD to my lord: sit at My right hand" (Psalms 110:1). "And Your humility has made me great" — what great humility, that He would sit while the Shechinah stood, as it is written (Genesis 18:1), "and the LORD appeared to him by the terebinths of Mamre, and he was sitting at the entrance of the tent." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:9: Further, they said in Megillah (31a), these are their words: Rabbi Yochanan said, wherever you find the might of the Holy One, blessed be He, you find His humility alongside it. This matter is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and tripled in the Writings. In the Torah (Deuteronomy 10:17), "for the LORD your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords," and it is written after it, "who executes justice for the orphan and the widow." Repeated in the Prophets, as it is said (Isaiah 57:15), "for thus says the High and Exalted One," and it is written after it, "and with the crushed and the humble of spirit." Tripled in the Writings, as it is written (Psalms 68:5), "extol Him who rides upon the clouds [aravot], whose name is Yah," and it is written after it, "a father of orphans and a judge of widows." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:10: And in the Yalkut (Isaiah §488) further verses are brought: (Psalms 146:6-7), "who made heaven and earth" etc., "who executes justice for the oppressed," and it is written (Isaiah 66:1), "the heavens are My throne" etc. "but to this one I look — to the poor and contrite in spirit." "The LORD is King forever and ever" (Psalms 10:16) — what is written after it? "You have heard the desire of the humble, O LORD" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:11: Further, they said in Sotah (5a) regarding the verse "and with the crushed and the humble of spirit": Rav Huna and Rav Chisda — one said, "I come [to] the crushed one," and one said, "I am with the crushed one." And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "I come [to] the crushed one" — I raise him up until he dwells with Me, this being "I shall dwell with the crushed one"; "I am with the crushed one" — I make My Shechinah rest beside him. And it seems reasonable according to the one who said "I am with the crushed one," for the Holy One, blessed be He, left all the mountains and hills and rested His Shechinah upon Mount Sinai, and Mount Sinai was not the highest. Rav Yosef said: a person should always learn from the mind of his Creator, for the Holy One, blessed be He, left all mountains and hills and rested His Shechinah upon Mount Sinai, and left all the good trees and rested His Shechinah in the thornbush. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:12: Now, in the plain interpretation apparent from these statements in tractates Megillah and Sotah, one finds humility above in the first three sefirot together with the Holy One, blessed be He, and further in the Shechinah, as will be explained — for the place of pride is in the first three sefirot, as is explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Pinchas, 223a), that David, when he reached the three supernal sefirot, opened and said (Psalms 131:1), "LORD, my heart is not proud, nor are my eyes haughty; I do not occupy myself with great matters, or with things too wondrous for me" — and this is what is meant by "for thus says the High and Exalted One" etc., this being said regarding Chochmah and Binah, as explained in the Zohar: "high" [ram] from Abraham, "exalted" [nissa] from Isaac. Likewise "I dwell in the high and holy place" is above, in the head of Arich [Anpin], where there is "holy," as explained in the Idra Naso (134a). And likewise "extol Him who rides upon the clouds, whose name is Yah," as this verse is explained in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 165a), where it is explained that "He who rides upon the clouds" is the supernal Mother; see there. And further, in tractate Sotah, that a person should learn from the mind of his Creator, who did not rest His Shechinah [on the tallest mountain] etc. — behold, humility in the Holy One, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:13: And the fullest presence of humility is found in the lower attribute, which is the Shechinah of the Holy One, blessed be He, called the Moon — and the Moon is destined in the future to be restored from its present diminishment of light. They said in tractate Chullin (60b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to her, righteous men shall be called by your name: Jacob the small, Samuel the small, David the small. David, because he was a chariot for this attribute, would make himself small and say, "I am young and despised" (Psalms 119:141), since sometimes the Moon is diminished; and sometimes he would make himself great: "the utterance of the man raised on high" etc. (2 Samuel 23:1). This is likewise explained in the Zohar (portion Pekudei, 232b), where it says that King David lowered himself before the Holy One, blessed be He — for whoever lowers himself before the Holy One, blessed be He, is raised above all — and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, was pleased with him in this world and in the World to Come. In this world (2 Kings 19:34), "and I will defend this city for My own sake and for the sake of David My servant"; in the World to Come, as it is written (Hosea 3:5), "and they shall seek the LORD their God and David their king" etc. — David is king in this world, and David shall be king in the time to come; and of this it says (Psalms 118:22), "the stone the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:14: Come and see: at the time the Moon's light is removed and it no longer shines, it is then in poverty on all sides, darkened, and has no light at all; and when the Sun turns toward it and illuminates it, then it adorns itself toward him like a female who adorns herself toward the male, and then it rules with dominion in the world. Therefore David crowned himself in exactly that manner — sometimes poor and sometimes wealthy, in the wealth of everything — and therefore he would say (ibid. 119:141), "I am young and despised, yet I have not forgotten Your precepts." In like manner, a person must lower himself in everything, in order to become a vessel in which the Holy One, blessed be He, is pleased — and this has already been established regarding "and with the crushed and humble of spirit." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:15: Therefore, the poor whose hearts are broken and crushed are a chariot for this attribute, and so it is explained in the Zohar (beginning of portion Vayikra, 9), these are his words: but come and see, no people of the world are found closer to the Supernal King than these vessels which He makes use of, and who are these? "A broken and crushed heart" (Psalms 51:19), "and with the crushed and humble of spirit" (Isaiah 57:15) — these are the King's vessels. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:16: And likewise it says in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, ch. 7) on the verse (Psalms 51:19), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit": these are his words: Rabbi Abba bar Marion said, everything the Holy One, blessed be He, disqualified in an animal, He made fit in a person: He disqualified in an animal blindness, a broken limb, a cut, or a wart, but made fit in a person "a broken and crushed heart." Rabbi Alexandri said, for an ordinary person, if he uses broken vessels it is a disgrace to him, but the Holy One, blessed be He, uses broken vessels, as it is said (ibid. 34:19), "the LORD is near to the brokenhearted," "He heals the brokenhearted" (ibid. 147:3), "and with the crushed and humble of spirit" (Isaiah 57:15), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken heart" (Psalms 51:19). Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:17: The general principle is that in all of Atzilut one finds humility, each level according to its own aspect. In Tikkunim (5b) it is explained that the Shechinah is called Humility, these are his words: and humility is bound with awe — this is what is written (Proverbs 22:4), "the reward of humility is the fear of the LORD" — whoever has the fear of the LORD is thereby brought to humility, which is the supernal Shechinah, for whom the fear of the LORD is the "heel" [i.e., the lowest attachment]; and this is the level of Moses, of whom it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" — and because awe is her "heel," the masters of the Mishnah established that awe is a small matter for Moses. Thus far his words. And in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Pinchas, 230a) it is explained that Malchut is called Humility, these are his words: and therefore the masters of the Mishnah established, "not study is the essential thing but deed" — for the Holy One, blessed be He, is hidden in the secrets of Torah, and by what is He known? By the commandment, which is the Shechinah, His image — just as He is humble, His Shechinah is humility; He is pious, and she is pious, etc. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:18: Further, one finds humility even in Keter, for the attributes of humility are that a person overlook his own affronts and be merciful, and the like, these being the thirteen attributes we mention: "the LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in kindness" etc. (Exodus 34:6), and likewise "who is a God like You, forgiving iniquity and overlooking transgression for the remnant of His inheritance" (Micah 7:18), which Rashbi explains in the Idra Naso (131b) as the thirteen attributes of mercy in Arich [Anpin]. Behold, wherever you find His greatness, even above, in the place of pride, there you find humility; therefore a person must resemble his Creator and overlook his own affronts and [emulate] the other qualities mentioned in the Holy One, blessed be He's thirteen attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:19: Likewise our Sages of blessed memory explained in the Midrash (Yalkut, portion Ekev §873, 283c), these are their words: "to walk in all His ways" — these are the ways of the Omnipresent: "the LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in kindness and truth" (Exodus 34:6), and it says (Joel 3:5), "whoever calls upon the name of the LORD shall be saved" — but how is it possible for a person to be called by the name of the LORD? Rather, the Omnipresent is called merciful and gracious, as it is said (Psalms 103:8), "merciful and gracious is the LORD" — you too be gracious and give gifts freely. The Omnipresent is called merciful, as it is said (Deuteronomy 4:31), "for the LORD your God is a merciful God" — you too be merciful. The Omnipresent is called righteous, as it is said (Psalms 11:7), "for the LORD is righteous, He loves righteousness" — you too be righteous. The Omnipresent is called pious [chasid], as it is said (Jeremiah 3:12), "I am pious, says the LORD" — you too be pious. Therefore it is said, "and it shall be that whoever calls upon the name of the LORD shall be saved," and it says (Proverbs 16:4), "the LORD has made everything for its own purpose." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:20: I have heard in the name of the Geonim that on this intent they said in tractate Rosh Hashanah (17b), on "and the LORD passed before him and proclaimed" (Exodus 34:6): Rabbi Yochanan said, were it not written in the verse, it would be impossible to say it — this teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, wrapped Himself [in a tallit] like a prayer leader and showed Moses [the order of the thirteen attributes], saying to him, whenever Israel does before Me according to this order, I will forgive them. Thus far his words. And this is difficult, for we see that many times we recite the Thirteen Attributes and they are not answered. Rather, the Geonim say that the intent of "do before Me according to this order" is not only about wrapping in a tallit, but that they should perform the order of the attributes that the Holy One, blessed be He, taught Moses — namely, "God, merciful and gracious" — meaning, just as He is merciful, you too be merciful, etc., and so for all thirteen attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:21: My teacher, peace be upon him, wrote that besides the aspect of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, which is the aspect of the thirteen corrections of the beard, which are explained as indicating humility, also all the other corrections of Arich Anpin, designated by the names head, forehead, eye, nose, mouth, etc., all indicate His great humility toward the creatures.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:22: From the attribute of the Head is humility, for it is said, "lowly of knee and light for the head" — meaning that a person lowers his head before one greater than himself, so the attribute of Keter lowers itself before the Cause above all; it is called "Ayin" [Nothing] because it considers itself as nothing before the Emanator, and it lowers its head to watch over and bestow upon the lower beings, all of whom turn to draw nourishment from it. Likewise it is fitting for a person to consider himself as nothing before His greatness, blessed be He, which has no end or limit, as we elaborated in the Gate of Awe, chapters 1-2, and of this Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Exodus 16:7), "and what are we?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:23: Likewise it is possible to say that for this reason Chochmah is called "MaH" [what], as explained in the Zohar (portion Yitro, 79b), "MaH is His name" — and besides the known reason, that it is the secret of the Name that adds up to MaH and is [the same numerical value as] ADaM, it is possible that for the reason mentioned it is called "MaH," since it considers itself as nothing [bilimah] before its Emanator, along the lines of "and all the inhabitants of the earth are considered as nothing" (Daniel 4:32).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:24: And just as no blemish from the lower beings prevents Keter from bestowing its flow, which never ceases, so too a person, even if they sin against him, should not thereby refrain from doing good, as we are commanded (Leviticus 19:18), "you shall not take revenge nor bear a grudge" — and it is already known what they explained (Yoma 23a) regarding revenge and grudge-bearing. We find, then, that according to the law of the Torah, a person is obligated to be humble and to have no grudge in his heart against his fellow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:25: The second, in the Brain: he must clear his thought of all confusion and disgust, and be attached to Torah, in the manner that thought is attached above to draw nourishment — regarding this Rashbi, peace be upon him, and his companions were careful never to cease their thought even for a moment, as is known.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:26: The third, in the Forehead: he must not be brazen-faced, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:3), "and you have had the forehead of a harlot woman" etc.; rather he should draw a continual flow of goodwill toward every person, just as the supernal forehead is called "the forehead of goodwill," through which the judgments in the lower worlds are appeased (portion Naso, 129a) — so no quarrel or dispute should be aroused from him toward any person, small or great, but rather all should be pleased with him, even non-Jews.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:27: In the Eyes: his eye must be open to have compassion on the poor and watch over them, just as regarding the supernal eye it is said (Psalms 33:18), "behold, the eye of the LORD is toward those who fear Him, toward those who wait for His kindness," and likewise, "behold, He who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps" (ibid. 121:4) — for He guards, watches, and has mercy forever, and even if the lower beings sin, He does not remove the watchfulness of His mercy from them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:28: Likewise one must be generous and giving with his money, and give with a good eye, and be one of a "good eye," for above, regarding the supernal eye it is said (Proverbs 22:9), "he who has a good eye shall be blessed" — and one who merits this attribute will live long, as they said in tractate Megillah, chapter "Bnei Ha'ir" (28a): they asked Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, through what did you lengthen your days? He said, I was generous with my money. The reason is that whoever is exacting indicates his own contraction, which is judgment in the secret of the "breakage" [shevirat hakelim]; but one who is generous indicates Chesed, which gives and grants freely even to one who is not deserving — and all the qualities of Arich [Anpin] indicate complete kindness and generosity without any exactingness at all, and there is the place of length of days; therefore he lengthens his days, measure for measure.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:29: Similarly they said of Job, that he was generous with his money. They said in Bava Batra, chapter 1 (15b): Rabbi Yochanan said, greater is what is said of Job than what is said of Abraham — for of Abraham it is written (Genesis 22:12), "for now I know that you fear God," and of Job it is written (Job 1:8), "a man perfect and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil." What is "turning away from evil"? They said, Job was generous with his money — the custom of the world is [to give] half a perutah to a shopkeeper [as a small tip], but Job would give a whole [perutah] from his own. Thus far his words. And one must say that "turning away from evil" means that he had a good eye, for one who is stingy is called "evil of eye," and since it says "turning away from evil," meaning from stinginess and an evil eye, and he was "good," the opposite of evil, he was generous with his money. Likewise Rabbi Perida, of whom it is explained in tractate Eruvin (54b), that he lengthened his days, living four hundred years, because he never got angry and taught the halakhah to his student four hundred times.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:30: Likewise, he must keep his eyes lowered, in the manner of the supernal eye, which is lowered and humble in bestowing upon the world — and we have further elaborated on the correction of the eyes in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 8.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:31: In the Ears: his ears should be open to hear the voice of Torah, the voice of prayer, and the voice of the poor, to have compassion on them; but he should not let them hear the voice of evil speech, idle words, and other things that blemish, as explained in the Gate of Holiness. And if he hears his own disgrace, he should not respond, for the Holy One, blessed be He, conceals His ear from the debts of people and does not repay them measure for measure — and of this they said in Sefer Heichalot (ch. 18, §4) that the angels call the Holy One, blessed be He, "the insulted King" — His insult being that He bestows goodness and life upon the creatures, and with what He gives them they sin before Him, and He bears it and is insulted.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:32: In the Nose: he should resemble the attribute of the supernal nose, of which it is said (Isaiah 48:9), "I will restrain My anger [echtom, related to nose] for My praise's sake, so as not to cut you off" — for He is slow to anger, and from Him flow and pour forth life and abundance to all the creatures; so should he resemble His attribute, blessed be He, and let no burning anger go forth from him toward any person.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:33: In the Face: he should resemble the attributes called "face," of which it is said (Numbers 6:25), "may the LORD make His face shine upon you" — he should receive every person with a pleasant countenance, and should never show a brazen face, God forbid, toward any person, as his punishment will be explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:34: In the Mouth: he should resemble the attribute of the supernal mouth, and not let curses, excommunications, bans, harsh and impudent words, or disgraceful speech come out of his mouth — for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi used to boast that he never excommunicated anyone in his life. These are his words in the Yerushalmi (Mo'ed Katan, ch. "Elu Megalchin," 1:1): Rabbi Yehoshua sent for a certain man three times and he did not come; he sent to him, "were it not that I have never excommunicated a person in my days, I would excommunicate that man" — for there are twenty-four things for which one is excommunicated for the honor of a teacher, and this is one of them: "and whoever does not come... according to the counsel of the officials and elders, all his property shall be forfeited and he shall be separated from the assembly of the exiles" (Ezra 10:8). Thus far his words. From this a person should learn not to let curses and blasphemies come out of his mouth, but his tongue should be gentle to all, small and great alike. And one who increases silence regarding worldly matters lengthens his days, since he thereby resembles his mouth to the attribute of the supernal mouth, as we have already elaborated in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 10; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:35: Although it has been explained that a person must conduct himself according to the attribute of his Creator regarding humility, sometimes he must also conduct himself with the attribute of judgment toward the wicked, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 139:21-22), "do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD, and loathe those who rise against You? I hate them with utmost hatred." And it is forbidden to have mercy on the wicked, as it is said (Proverbs 12:10), "and the mercies of the wicked are cruel." We likewise find a deed done by Rabbi Chanina, who did not have mercy on a wicked man. They said in Vayikra Rabbah (5:6): Rabbi Ibo said, there was a certain butcher in Tzippori who used to feed Israel non-kosher and torn meat; once, on the eve of Yom Kippur, he ate and drank and became drunk, and went up onto the roof and fell and died. Dogs began licking his blood, and they asked Rabbi Chanina whether it was permitted to drive them away from him. He said to them, "and you shall be holy men to Me... and flesh torn by beasts in the field you shall not eat; you shall throw it to the dogs" (Exodus 22:30) — this one, who used to rob the dogs and feed Israel non-kosher and torn meat, let him go — from their own [that he stole from them], they now eat. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:36: Likewise, sometimes he must rebuke one who needs rebuke, as King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 17:10), "a rebuke goes deeper into a man of understanding" etc. And likewise to discipline his son and his student, as it says (ibid. 13:24), "he who spares his rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently." But he must do so with a settled mind, without anger, thinking rather that this beating he gives his son or student is an act of kindness done for him, to draw him near to holiness and subdue the kelipah from him. And so they said (Arachin 16b): how many times was Akiva ben Yosef struck by me, and it added to him nothing but love — to fulfill what is said (ibid. 9:8), "rebuke a wise man and he will love you." And King David, peace be upon him, likewise said (Psalms 141:5), "let the righteous strike me — it is kindness; let him rebuke me" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:37: Likewise, if he is angry at his fellow who has treated him unjustly, he should remember some good his fellow has done for him, so that his anger be relieved, and learn from the attribute of his Creator, as it is said in tractate Berachot (54b): Rabbi Yochanan said, even at the time of the Holy One, blessed be He's anger, He remembers the righteous, as it is said (Genesis 19:29), "and it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham" — what remembrance? He remembered for Lot's sake the silence that Abraham kept, when he said of Sarah, "she is my sister" (cf. Genesis 12:13), and he [Lot] knew and kept silent. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:38: This is one of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy that the prophet mentioned in "who is a God like You" (Micah 7:18) — one of them being that He suppresses our iniquities, the intent being that although by rights the litigants should go forth to exact payment from whoever committed that sin, the Holy One, blessed be He, suppresses them under His hand and remembers some good deed [the sinner has done]; likewise a person should conduct himself with his fellow, remembering his good deed and suppressing the wrong he did to him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:39: Further, among the attributes of humility are the three things we learn in tractate Avot (5:19): whoever possesses these three things is among the disciples of Abraham our father — a good eye, a humble spirit, and a lowly soul, etc. Most commentators agree that "a good eye" means being content with what one has, and even if his fellow has more money than he, he does not envy him, but his own little seems much to him, and others' [wealth] seems little to him, and he wishes that they have even more than he would wish for himself. Its opposite is "an evil eye" — his eye is stingy regarding what his fellow has, and his own, even though it is much, seems little to him, while his fellow's, even if little, seems much to him — this is envy, that he envies what his fellow has and his eye is evil regarding what he himself has, wishing that he have little, so long as his fellow has even less.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:40: "A humble spirit" is great humility, and its opposite is pride, which is a "haughty spirit" — and we find pride called "spirit" [ruach], as it says (Ezekiel 20:32), "and what comes into your mind [ruach]" [in a context of arrogant plans].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:41: "A lowly soul" is to distance oneself from desire, not pursuing the fulfillment of his craving in matters of food and forbidden relations. We find that desire is called "soul" [nefesh], as it says (Deuteronomy 12:20), "according to all the desire of your soul," and "whatever your soul asks of you" (ibid. 14:26). "A broad soul" is its opposite — one who pursues his desire, as it says (Ecclesiastes 6:7), "yet the soul [appetite] is not filled." And one who pursues desire in food and other matters, his heart becomes proud, as it is written (Deuteronomy 8:12), "lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses and dwell in them... and your heart become proud and you forget the LORD your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:42: This path was explained by Rambam, and the other commentators followed after him. And Rabbi Yitzchak Abravanel, in his commentary on the Mishnah, explained this matter and expanded upon it, saying that these three correspond to the three things mentioned by Rabbi Elazar HaKappar: envy, desire, and honor. Envy corresponds to "an evil eye" — his eye is evil regarding what others have, and he envies them; this falls in the matter of money, until because of this he comes to covetousness, robbery, theft, fraud, and all the transgressions bound up with the acquisition of money. Corresponding to desire is "a broad soul," which is excessive desire for intercourse, food, and other forbidden things. Corresponding to honor is "a haughty spirit," for when a person is proud and arrogant, he comes to disgrace and curse his fellow and to honor himself through his fellow's shame.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:43: From Rambam's interpretation, and likewise Rabbi Yitzchak Abravanel's, it appears that their version of the Mishnah read "a good eye, a lowly soul, and a haughty spirit" — matching exactly the order of envy, desire, and honor, as explained. But our version is not so — nor is the version of the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him — but rather "a good eye, a humble spirit, and a lowly soul," and this version appears to be primary, for the reason we shall explain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:44: These three were found in Abraham our father, and their opposites in the wicked Balaam, as Rambam and Rabbi Yitzchak Abravanel explained thoroughly; see there. Since it does not pertain to practical matters, we have not copied their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:45: According to our approach, these three attributes mentioned are found in His attributes, blessed and exalted be He, above in His holy and pure Atzilut. "A good eye" is giving with generosity and abundance, and we have already explained above that there is an attribute called "he who has a good eye shall be blessed," and this designation may be applied to the first three sefirot, since their bestowal is with mercy and generosity — for it is known that Imma [the supernal Mother] is called "the treasury of gifts given freely," as our Sages of blessed memory explained (Devarim Rabbah 2:1) regarding "Va'etchanan" (Deuteronomy 6:23), that he asked from the treasury of free gifts, of which it is said (Exodus 33:19), "and I will be gracious to whomever I will be gracious," even though he is not deserving or fitting.
